result:
The city at three in the morning is a different organism entirely. I mean this in the literal sense. The rhythm of it shifts from something you walk through to something that walks through you.

There are fewer sounds, but the sounds that remain are magnified. A delivery truck sliding across wet asphalt. The particular groan of a train on elevated tracks, the one that carries no passengers, just empty cars rattling through the dark. A dog barking twice at nothing, at nothing it will never explain, and then silence again, thicker still.

The streetlights have a quality they don't possess at noon. They pull long gold rectangles across the pavement and you walk through them like frames in a film. The glass of a bodega window holds the whole night in it, and behind that glass a man is watching television, his face blue and small, and he is the only witness to the fact that this city still exists while everyone else is dreaming it away.

I think that's what it is, actually. The city exists because someone is awake to hold it in place. At three in the morning the weight of holding falls on very few shoulders. The night-shift nurse. The baker already elbow-deep in dough. The insomniac in the apartment above, hearing the water pipes sing.

And you, if you're out there, are one of them. A small candle in a very large, very dark room. Not illuminating anything. Just refusing, quietly, to go out.

"The city at three in the morning is a different organism entirely. I mean this in the literal sense. The rhythm of it shifts from something you walk through to something that walks through you.

There are fewer sounds, but the sounds that remain are magnified. A delivery truck sliding across wet asphalt. The particular groan of a train on elevated tracks, the one that carries no passengers, just empty cars rattling through the dark. A dog barking twice at nothing, at nothing it will never explain, and then silence again, thicker still.

The streetlights have a quality they don't possess at noon. They pull long gold rectangles across the pavement and you walk through them like frames in a film. The glass of a bodega window holds the whole night in it, and behind that glass a man is watching television, his face blue and small, and he is the only witness to the fact that this city still exists while everyone else is dreaming it away.

I think that's what it is, actually. The city exists because someone is awake to hold it in place. At three in the morning the weight of holding falls on very few shoulders. The night-shift nurse. The baker already elbow-deep in dough. The insomniac in the apartment above, hearing the water pipes sing.

And you, if you're out there, are one of them. A small candle in a very large, very dark room. Not illuminating anything. Just refusing, quietly, to go out."
